Anthropic is applying the watermark to American users: "wherever Claude is offered, worldwide." Google has been watermarking Gemini text since 2024, and OpenAI says its goal is to "expand provenance signals to all modalities including text." No federal US law requires these watermarks in AI generated text. Anthropic is applying the EU requirement in the US anyways. OpenAI published a post supporting the same EU code in June without mentioning text watermarking. It mentioned text only later, in one sentence, without saying how or when the marking would be added. People are cancelling their Claude subscriptions over this, yet most of the alternatives signed the same EU code. OpenAI, Google, Meta, Microsoft and Mistral all signed. SpaceXAI has not. If you want to avoid this, open models are looking a lot more attractive.

tweets.text: RT @neil_chilson: The EU is pressing an invisible thumbprint onto every response Anthropic models produce, anywhere in the world. Anthropic announced yesterday that it is embedding a watermark directly into Claude-generated text. Because the company weaves the mark into the words themselves, it persists through copy and paste and can survive later editing. Anthropic plans to stamp this mark on Claude, Claude Code, its API, cloud platforms, and its other products, in Europe and everywhere else. This is the Brussels Effect, one token at a time. Article 50 of the EU AI Act has pushed a leading American AI company to alter every text response its covered models generate, worldwide. Counted in tokens, this may be the most expansive government intrusion into expressive content in history. Anthropic claims the watermark will not affect meaning, quality, or readability. But it reportedly works by hiding a detectable signal in the model's word choices. If a detector can find that signal, the signal changed which words the model chose. So the model now attempts to optimize for two things at once: the best response for the user, and a regulator-facing signal buried inside it. The mark limits the output relative to what the model would otherwise produce, and that reduces quality, even if users rarely notice. The mandate originates in Europe, but Anthropic chose to implement it worldwide. A student in Ohio, a programmer in India, and a small business in Argentina will all carry an EU-mandated mark on what they produce. No law requires that. Anthropic's choice to impose an EU law on all of us deserves significant scrutiny and public pressure. Especially because the mark also fails to do its job. Anthropic acknowledges that a human may have written a marked passage and asked Claude only to proofread, translate, or summarize it. Meanwhile, ordinary editing can strip the mark from text that Claude wrote in full. The mark is therefore both overinclusive and evadable, flagging human work while missing machine work. No teacher, editor, or employer should judge authorship, credibility, academic integrity, or effort on a signal that weak. Transparency rules can be worth it when they tell people something useful. This one reveals little and yet requires a change to every output. EU policymakers should narrow Article 50's treatment of ordinary text and focus on concrete abuses: fraud, impersonation, and harmful deepfakes. Anthropic should apply the mark only where the law demands it, and better still, let users choose. Having struggled to export their technology to the world, Europe's regulators have long sought to export their regulations. The U.S. should push back. We shouldn't have to have European fingerprints on every American sentence that AI touches.
